analysis.one_liner: Requires oceangoing ships entering U.S. ports to burn low-sulfur fuel and install stronger pollution controls.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have cut smog-forming ship exhaust near U.S. ports, never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Ships that dock at U.S. ports burn some of the dirtiest fuel available, and their exhaust drifts into nearby neighborhoods. This bill would have directed the EPA to require those vessels — including foreign-flagged ships — to use fuel with far less sulfur starting in 2010, and to set tough standards for engine pollution starting in 2012. It was introduced by Representative Hilda Solis with 23 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work near ports — in port cities like Los Angeles, Long Beach, New York, and Houston — breathe ship exhaust that carries sulfur dioxide and fine particles linked to asthma, heart disease, and premature death. The bill would have required ships within 200 miles of the West Coast, and similar distances elsewhere, to cut that pollution beginning at the end of 2010, and required new engines to achieve the maximum emission reduction available technology allows beginning in 2012. Cleaner air near ports, and progress toward federal air-quality deadlines that many port regions were missing, would have been the payoff [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Required marine vessels, including foreign-flagged ships, to use fuel with no more than 1,000 parts per million of sulfur in their main and auxiliary engines starting December 31, 2010, whenever they are within 200 miles of the West Coast or within a distance the EPA sets for the East Coast, Gulf Coast, Great Lakes, and St. Lawrence Seaway [S2] [S3].

Required the EPA to set standards for nitrogen oxides, particulate matter, hydrocarbons, and carbon monoxide from oceangoing vessel engines, with new engines achieving the greatest emission reduction available technology allows beginning January 1, 2012, and a second round of maximum-control standards beginning January 1, 2016 if stricter technology is not ready by 2012 [S2] [S3].

Allowed an alternative compliance path for ships that install scrubbing technology achieving equivalent pollution cuts, and let the EPA set an interim sulfur limit (capped at 2,000 ppm) if full compliance was not technically feasible by the 2010 deadline — flexibility meant to keep the standard achievable [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ocean shipping companies would have paid for low-sulfur fuel, which costs more than the heavy bunker fuel most ships burn, and for engine upgrades or scrubbers. Those costs would flow through shipping rates to the price of goods moved by sea. Refiners would have had to produce lower-sulfur marine fuel. The bill's findings argue current controls are inadequate to protect public health, framing the compliance cost as the price of reducing a health burden that falls on port communities [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Shipping costs would rise: low-sulfur marine fuel is more expensive than conventional bunker fuel, and the bill applied to foreign-flagged vessels, meaning U.S. importers and consumers would bear some of the added freight cost [S2] [S3].

The bill's own flexibility provisions concede the risk that the technology and fuel supply might not be ready — it let the EPA delay to an interim 2,000 ppm standard if full compliance was not technically feasible by 2010, an acknowledgment the deadlines were aggressive [S2] [S3].

Requiring controls only on ships entering U.S. ports could impose costs on vessels calling at U.S. ports that competitors serving other countries avoid, raising fair-competition concerns the bill does not directly address [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes were significant: ship exhaust is a major source of sulfur and soot in port regions that were struggling to meet federal air-quality deadlines, and the bill's own findings said existing controls were inadequate to protect public health [S3]. The costs — pricier fuel and engine retrofits, passed partly into shipping rates — were real but modest per unit of goods shipped, and the bill built in feasibility escape valves. The honest objection is less about the cost than about one country acting alone on ships that operate worldwide; a coordinated international standard would spread the same compliance burden more evenly.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Hilda Solis introduced the bill on May 24, 2007, joined by original cosponsors including Representatives Harman, Capps, and Waxman, and 23 Democratic cosponsors in total signed on [S1] [S3] [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, which referred it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, on the same day it was introduced [S5].

No further action appears in the record: the subcommittee and full committee never reported the bill, and it never reached the House floor before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ocean shipping lines and marine fuel suppliers were better off, because they avoided the cost of low-sulfur fuel and engine retrofits that the bill would have required. Port-area residents continued to bear the ship exhaust the bill targeted.

for.name: Rep. Hilda L. Solis
for.role: Sponsor; House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the EPA to require low-sulfur ship fuel and stricter marine engine emission standards.

for.name: 23 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Reps. Harman, Capps, and Waxman; none of the bill's support came from Republicans.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: Original cosponsor; senior Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never held a markup or reported it to the floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality
against.role: Subcommittee of referral, chaired by Rep. Rick Boucher (D-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no recorded action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 supporters — the sponsor and 23 cosponsors — were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsor; the committee that buried it was chaired by a Democrat, so the inaction was a committee decision rather than a straight partisan floor fight.

industries.note: Ships entering U.S. ports would have had to buy lower-sulfur fuel and meet engine standards, raising operating costs; the savings from avoiding those requirements come at the expense of air quality in port neighborhoods.

Refiners would have faced costs to produce marine fuel with no more than 1,000 ppm sulfur, but would have sold that fuel to a captive shipping market. Whether they netted gains or losses depends on how costs passed through.

The bill created demand for engine upgrades and exhaust-cleaning technology, including an alternative compliance path for ships that install scrubbers achieving equivalent cuts. Its benefits run with the public's cleaner air.
